after: The variety of living things found in one region
purpose: Distinguish the number of individuals from the number of kinds recorded.
paragraphs: Suppose you record eighteen ants of one kind, two crows and one squirrel. That is twenty-one animals, but only three kinds in your record. Counting individuals answers “How many animals?” Counting kinds answers a different question. Neither count tells you what your search missed.
anchorText: The variety of living things found in one region is called its **biodiversity**.

after: Removing a tree can remove shade
purpose: Explain how an arrow represents a specific resource, without implying every relationship is mutual.
paragraphs: An arrow labelled “shelter” from a tree to a bird describes what the tree provides. It does not mean that the bird shelters the tree in return. If you want to show another relationship, draw another labelled arrow. One pair of living things may be connected in several ways.
anchorText: Removing a tree can remove shade, nest sites and a source of fallen leaves. The effects depend on which organisms use it and what other resources are available nearby.

after: How would a library arranged by book size
purpose: Make an imprecise grouping rule operational and testable by another group.
paragraphs: Make “large leaves” precise: try “longer than 10 cm from base to tip”. State where a leaf exactly 10 cm long belongs, so another group can repeat your sorting.
anchorText: How would a library arranged by book size help a reader? What would be harder to find?

after: Climbing and trailing describe growth habits
purpose: Distinguish a climber from its support when two plants overlap.
paragraphs: A climber growing over another plant can look like part of it. Trace one visible stem with your eyes from its base towards its leaves. Which leaves belong to that stem, and which belong to the support? Sketch the two separately. Observe without tugging: pulling them apart could damage both plants.
anchorText: Climbing and trailing describe growth habits, not a separate woody/non-woody division. A grape vine is a woody climber; a pumpkin has non-woody trailing stems. A plant can therefore be described in more than one way.

after: Compare veins separately from leaf outlines
purpose: Use repeated rubbings to distinguish a specimen feature from a recording artefact.
paragraphs: Make two rubbings of the same fallen leaf, changing only the pencil pressure. Compare both with the leaf itself. A dark line in one print is not necessarily a thicker vein: it may show where you pressed harder. Use the leaf to decide which lines belong in your final record.
anchorText: Compare veins separately from leaf outlines: different outlines can share a vein pattern. Point to the lines supporting your grouping so others can follow your rule without knowing the plant names.

after: These two patterns help you compare
purpose: Show how to inspect the network beyond the midrib when identifying venation.
paragraphs: Do not stop at the thick middle vein. Follow several smaller veins towards the edge and look between them. In a net-like pattern, branches join to enclose small areas. In a parallel pattern, the main veins run alongside one another. Describe the overall arrangement, rather than deciding from one short line.
anchorText: These two patterns help you compare many of the leaves around you. Look closely: real leaves sometimes show exceptions.

after: Record age from germination
purpose: Apply the age-control instruction to a concrete comparison without giving an investigation result.
paragraphs: Imagine that seedling A germinated on Monday and seedling B on Wednesday. A drawing of both on Friday compares different ages. To compare them at the same age, use the record of A two days after germination and the record of B two days after germination. Keep the dates beside both drawings.
anchorText: Record age from germination as well as the date. On Friday, seeds that germinated on Monday and Thursday are at different stages. Compare similar-aged seedlings before attributing a difference to the kind of plant.

after: Both root systems anchor plants
purpose: Prevent learners from mistaking side branches of a taproot for a fibrous system.
paragraphs: A taproot system may have many thin side roots, so counting roots alone can mislead you. Look for where they join. Do smaller roots branch from a clear main root, or do several roots arise near the stem base? Trace these connections in the specimen or diagram before choosing a description.
anchorText: Both root systems anchor plants and take up water and dissolved minerals. Their branching patterns differ; their jobs overlap.

after: Table 2.4: Sample leaf and root record
purpose: Explain the sample row without confusing a recorded observation with a prior prediction.
paragraphs: The lemongrass row records parallel veins and fibrous roots, but no prediction. For your fifth plant, keep the prediction and later observation in separate columns so another reader can compare them.
anchorText:

Plant | Venation | Root prediction (fifth plant) | Root observed
Lemongrass | Parallel |  | Fibrous

after: Pool the class records.
purpose: Explain how uncertain results affect the number of usable tests of a prediction.
paragraphs: Suppose four predictions were checked: three matched, and one plant had broken roots. You have three matches and one uncertain result, not four matches. Report both numbers. The uncertain plant needs another observation; leaving it out without explanation would make the pattern appear better supported than your records show.
anchorText: Pool the class records. Count how many support a connection and how many do not. Compare the result with these common patterns in flowering plants.

after: Which seed comes apart neatly
purpose: Prepare readers to interpret the section diagram without using size to name seed structures.
paragraphs: The maize picture is a lengthwise section: it shows parts hidden inside the grain. Follow each label to its endpoint. A part’s size alone cannot tell you whether it is a cotyledon.
anchorText: Which seed comes apart neatly into two halves? Which one does not?

after: If seed anatomy identifies a plant as a monocot
purpose: Explain two distinct reading directions and the limits of a table of typical features.
paragraphs: Read across the cotyledon row to compare the two groups using the same feature. Read down the monocot column to connect several features of that group. Each direction answers a different question. The table summarises typical patterns; it does not replace observations of the particular plant in front of you.
anchorText: If seed anatomy identifies a plant as a monocot, you can predict that it is likely to have parallel venation and fibrous roots. Check those features before claiming the prediction is correct.

after: Use your animal records as a starting point.
purpose: Model recording successive actions rather than treating one moment as an animal’s complete movement range.
paragraphs: For example, a pigeon might walk along a wall, pause, then fly away. Record the actions in order and name the body parts used for each moving stage. The pause is part of your observation too, but it does not show how the bird moves. Separate what happened from what the animal might be able to do.
anchorText: Use your animal records as a starting point. Add observations from direct watching or a reliable video, and identify which source you used.

after: Different animals may move alike
purpose: Clarify that overlapping groups do not represent additional animals.
paragraphs: A record can belong in both “uses legs” and “uses wings”. If a class observed four animals, the two groups might contain six entries because two animals appear in both. That does not mean six animals were observed. Keep each animal’s name attached to its entries so you can recognise the overlap.
anchorText: Different animals may move alike using similar body parts: a housefly and a pigeon both fly with wings. A fish and a dolphin look alike in water, although a dolphin is not a fish.

after: Compare the warm sandy desert and cold mountain conditions
purpose: Prevent one example in a region column from being read as an exhaustive inventory.
paragraphs: Table 2.6 gives one example for each named setting. An empty space does not mean that no living things occur there, and one entry does not mean that only that kind occurs there. Add locally known examples with a source for each. Distinguish a direct sighting from a name supplied by a book.
anchorText: Compare the warm sandy desert and cold mountain conditions in your class table. Which conditions differ? What else would you need to know before predicting whether an animal could survive in both?

after: These features were not chosen by individual plants.
purpose: Work through the link between a structure, its effect, and the conditions in which it helps.
paragraphs: Connect a feature to an effect and then to a condition. For the cactus: a fleshy stem stores water; stored water can be used between rains. “It lives in a desert” names a setting but does not explain the feature. The fuller explanation shows why that feature can matter when water is scarce.
anchorText: These features were not chosen by individual plants. They are inherited features found in populations living in particular conditions. Other plants may survive there using different features.

after: Habitats can be small.
purpose: Help learners relate an organism’s location to specific resources within a habitat.
paragraphs: On a simple map of your observation area, mark a water source, a shaded patch and open ground. Add the positions where living things were seen. The map may suggest questions about shelter, moisture or food. It cannot show a preference from one sighting, but it helps you choose places to observe again.
anchorText: Habitats can be small. Damp soil beneath a log differs from a dry path beside it, helping explain why neighbouring places hold different living things.

after: **5.** Sort these animals
purpose: Extend the grouping assessment with a checkable rule and an ambiguous case.
paragraphs: Ask a partner to apply your rule without seeing your list. Compare the results and clarify any ambiguous wording or missing feature. The groups do not have to contain equal numbers of animals.
anchorText: **5.** Sort these animals into two groups, using any feature *not* used in this chapter — cow, cockroach, pigeon, bat, tortoise, whale, fish, grasshopper, lizard. Write your rule clearly.

after: **9.** A plant grows on an open
purpose: Extend the adaptation question into evidence planning without supplying its answer.
paragraphs: Plan a comparison using several plants of the same kind in each place. Name two conditions besides wind that you would record. Explain why a single tall plant and a single short plant would be weaker evidence than a repeated pattern across many similar-aged plants.
anchorText: **9.** A plant grows on an open, windy hilltop. It is short, with small tough leaves. The same kind of plant grows in a sheltered valley below. There it is twice as tall, with bigger leaves. Suggest how wind and shelter could affect its growth. Explain why this observation alone does not prove that a new inherited *adaptation* has developed.

after: **10.** A duck and a pigeon
purpose: Require a feature-function explanation to identify evidence and limits.
paragraphs: Support your explanation with a labelled sketch and an observation from a safe distance or a reliable video. Distinguish what the picture shows about the foot from what watching the bird shows about movement. Which part of your explanation is still a prediction that needs checking?
anchorText: **10.** A duck and a pigeon are both birds. But their feet are different. Describe the difference. What can the duck do because of it?
